learn: Definitions of agentic AI, and how agents differ from chatbots and from generative AI
Agent components: the LLM reasoning core, memory types, planning, tools and the action loop
Distributed transactions, the SAGA pattern and compensating transactions
SAGA orchestration vs choreography (AWS Step Functions, EventBridge)
SAGA orchestration for multi-agent systems (supervisor agents)
The blackboard pattern for multi-agent problem solving
intro.why: Agentic systems take real actions across many services. Without coordination patterns, a half-finished multi-step task leaves the world inconsistent.

symbols: reason + act loop: think, call a tool, observe, repeat
knowledge source (specialist) in the blackboard pattern

sections.title: What agentic AI is
sections.plain: From systems that answer to systems that get things done.
sections.body:
Definitions. Nvidia: "Agentic AI uses sophisticated reasoning and iterative planning to autonomously solve complex, multi-step problems." OpenAI: agentic systems "can pursue complex goals with limited direct supervision." A research definition: a foundation-model-based system that performs tasks (possibly producing artifacts) from natural instructions, able to conduct and express complex reasoning, including planning and reflection, for tasks requiring interaction with an environment or elaborate tool use.

Traditional AI / chatbotAgentic AI
Responds to prompts; single-turn; no tool use; statelessPursues goals over time; multi-step reasoning; uses tools and APIs; has memory and context

Timeline: 2017 Transformer architecture → 2020 GPT-3 → 2022 ChatGPT → 2023 early agents (AutoGPT, BabyAGI) → 2024–25 production-grade agentic systems.

Scenarios: trip planning (tips vs searching flights, comparing, booking and adding to the calendar); inbox (a template reply vs continuously reading, drafting, flagging urgent mail, unsubscribing and filing receipts); bug fixing (pasting code back and forth vs reading the repository, writing a fix, running tests, iterating and opening a pull request); research (answers from training data vs searching 40+ live sources and returning a cited summary in minutes); running an online store (reorder advice vs monitoring inventory, emailing suppliers and creating purchase orders).

Generative vs agentic. Generative AI: "tell me what to do, I'll generate an answer." Agentic AI: "give me a goal, I'll figure out the steps, act, and improve until it's done." Generative AI + reasoning + tools + feedback loops → agentic AI.

sections.title: Components of an agent
sections.plain: A reasoning LLM plus memory, planning, tools and a loop.
sections.body:
ComponentRole
LLM coreReasoning, language understanding, decisions
MemoryShort-term (context window) and long-term (e.g. a vector database)
PlanningTask decomposition, goal-oriented reasoning, delegation to sub-agents
Tool useAPIs, web search, code execution, file I/O, databases
Action loopObserve → think → act → reflect (ReAct pattern)

The LLM as reasoning engine: chain-of-thought reasoning, instruction following, generalisation to new tasks without retraining, tool use through JSON/API calls, and self-correction.

Memory typeHoldsCharacter
In-context / workingThe current context windowLost at the end of the session
External / episodicPast interactions in a vector DBUser-specific, dynamic
Semantic / knowledge baseFacts, rules, domain knowledgeRelatively static, global
Procedural / skillsHow to do things: system prompts, tool definitions, functions/APIs, workflowsDefines capabilities

Tools: web search (search APIs, fetching, scraping), code execution (a Python sandbox), file system, databases (SQL, vector, key-value), external APIs (email, calendar, payments, IoT) and other sub-agents. Calls are structured, and their results return into the context.

sections.title: Structured tool calls
sections.plain: The model emits JSON naming a tool and arguments; the runtime executes it and returns the result.
sections.body:
{"tool_name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Bangalore"}}
→ {"tool_result": "Temperature is 28°C"}

The model never executes anything itself: it proposes a call matching a declared schema; the host program validates, runs the tool, and appends the result to the conversation so the model can continue reasoning. Schemas make calls parseable and checkable, and are the place to enforce permissions.

sections.title: Distributed transactions, SAGA and compensating transactions
sections.plain: A chain of local commits with an undo action for each.
sections.body:
Distributed transaction: an e-commerce order spans services: Create Order (T1) → Process Payment (T2) → Update Inventory (T3) → Deliver Order (T4). Either all complete, or the preceding ones must be rolled back.

SAGA pattern: a sequence of local transactions; each updates its own database and publishes a message or event that triggers the next. If a step fails, the SAGA runs compensating transactions that undo the changes of the preceding steps.

$$T_1,\dots,T_n \text{ committed},\; T_{n+1}\text{ fails} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{run } C_n, C_{n-1},\dots,C_1$$

Automatic rollback is impossible because each step has already committed in its own service; compensation is a semantic undo (refund, restore stock, cancel order). Code example ex1 shows a courier failure at T4 triggering C3, C2, C1, and an insufficient-funds failure at T2 triggering only C1.

sections.title: SAGA orchestration vs choreography
sections.plain: One conductor, or dancers reacting to each other.
sections.body:
OrchestrationChoreography
A central orchestrator tells participants which local transactions to run; it handles all transactions, stores and interprets states, and handles failure recovery with compensations.Participants exchange events through a broker without a central point of control; each service knows which events to react to and what to publish.
Example: AWS Step Functions: create order → update inventory → make payment; on failure: refund payment, restore inventory, cancel/delete order.Example: Amazon EventBridge: order event → reserve inventory → payment rule → authorise payment → shipping rule → shipping service.
+ clear flow, central monitoring; − orchestrator is a bottleneck/single point of failure, coupling to it+ loose coupling, independent scaling; − implicit flow, harder to trace, risk of cyclic dependencies

sections.title: SAGA orchestration for multi-agent systems
sections.plain: A supervisor agent decomposes the task and delegates to specialists.
sections.body:
Problem: a multi-step task performed by several agents, each with its own state, tools and memory, must stay coordinated and recoverable.

Orchestration in agents: a central orchestrator (supervisor) agent decomposes the task and delegates to specialised worker agents (research, coding, summarisation, review). In Amazon Bedrock a supervisor agent coordinates agents that each have action groups (Lambda functions, a data warehouse, external APIs) and knowledge bases.

Demo: research-paper processing
  1. Orchestrator sends the paper to the validation agent → VALID / INVALID.
  2. If valid, the review agent lists strengths, weaknesses and suggestions.
  3. The summary agent writes a 300-word summary.
  4. State is persisted after each step; on failure, compensating actions run in reverse order.

sections.title: SAGA choreography and prompt chaining
sections.plain: Each step's output triggers the next; flawed steps are retried, reverted or refined.
sections.body:
Choreography for agents corresponds to the prompt-chaining pattern: hypothesis → plan → execute subtask (with tools or knowledge) → refine/revisit. When an intermediate result is flawed: retry differently, revert and re-plan, or use an evaluator loop (the evaluator-optimizer pattern, where one model critiques and another revises).

In Bedrock, agents with action groups (reserve inventory, order shipping, payments API) can be chained this way. Choreography demo: event-driven agents publish VALIDATED, REVIEWED and SUMMARIZED events to a shared event store; each agent reacts to the event it needs. On failure, agents publish compensation events processed in reverse order.

sections.title: The blackboard pattern
sections.plain: Specialists around a shared board add partial solutions until the problem is solved.
sections.body:
For problems with no well-defined algorithm: imagine experts around a blackboard, each adding a partial solution when they can.

ComponentRole
BlackboardGlobal data structure holding partial solutions, intermediate results and control information
Knowledge sources $KS_1\dots KS_n$Independent specialists (agents) that read from and write to the blackboard
Control component (controller/scheduler)Monitors the blackboard, selects which knowledge source acts next, resolves conflicts, controls execution until a solution is output

Demo: blackboard.json holds the paper text, validation, review comments, summary and status. The validation, review and summary agents each act only when their precondition is met; the scheduler loops until the status is COMPLETED or REJECTED. Agents never call each other. Code example ex2 implements exactly this.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "Agents are just chatbots with more tokens." The difference is the loop: tools, memory and acting on the world.
  • "Compensation = rollback." Compensation is a new forward action; some effects (an email sent) can't be undone and need a follow-up (an apology email), so put irreversible steps last.
  • Idempotency: agents and SAGA steps may be retried, so actions should be safe to repeat (use request IDs).
  • Guardrails: limit tool permissions, add human approval for irreversible actions, cap loop iterations and cost.

code.title: Blackboard with three agents and a controller
code.explain: Validation, review and summary knowledge sources act when their preconditions hold; the controller selects an eligible source each cycle until COMPLETED or REJECTED.
mistakes: Agents calling each other directly (defeats the pattern).
No termination condition in the controller.
code.notes: Replace each rule-based function with an LLM call that reads and writes the same JSON fields.
code.code:
"""Blackboard pattern with three 'agents' and a controller.

Agents never call each other. Each reads the shared blackboard, acts only when its
precondition holds, and writes a partial result. The controller loops, picks an
eligible knowledge source, and stops when the status is COMPLETED or REJECTED.
The agents here are simple rule-based stand-ins for LLM calls.
"""
import re, json

def validation_agent(bb):
    words = len(bb["paper"].split()); has_sections = all(s in bb["paper"].lower() for s in ("abstract", "method", "result"))
    bb["validation"] = "VALID" if words > 40 and has_sections else "INVALID"
    if bb["validation"] == "INVALID": bb["status"] = "REJECTED"

def review_agent(bb):
    p = bb["paper"].lower()
    bb["review"] = {
        "strengths": [s for s, k in [("quantitative results", r"\d+(\.\d+)?%"), ("baseline comparison", "baseline")] if re.search(k, p)],
        "weaknesses": [w for w, k in [("no ablation study", "ablation"), ("no limitations section", "limitation")] if k not in p],
    }

def summary_agent(bb):
    body = re.sub(r"\b(Abstract|Method|Results)\.\s*", "", bb["paper"]).strip()
    sents = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", body)
    bb["summary"] = " ".join(sents[:2])[:300]; bb["status"] = "COMPLETED"

KNOWLEDGE_SOURCES = [  # (name, precondition, action)
    ("validation", lambda b: b["validation"] is None, validation_agent),
    ("review",     lambda b: b["validation"] == "VALID" and b["review"] is None, review_agent),
    ("summary",    lambda b: b["review"] is not None and b["summary"] is None, summary_agent),
]

def controller(paper):
    bb = {"paper": paper, "validation": None, "review": None, "summary": None, "status": "IN_PROGRESS"}
    for cycle in range(1, 10):
        if bb["status"] in ("COMPLETED", "REJECTED"): break
        ready = [ks for ks in KNOWLEDGE_SOURCES if ks[1](bb)]
        if not ready: bb["status"] = "STUCK"; break
        name, _, act = ready[0]; act(bb)
        print(f"  cycle {cycle}: controller selects {name:<10} -> status {bb['status']}")
    return bb

good = ("Abstract. We propose a lightweight method for detecting defects in solar panels from drone images. "
        "Method. A pruned convolutional network is trained on 12,000 labelled images. "
        "Results. It reaches 94.1% recall versus 88.7% for the strongest baseline while running 3x faster on edge hardware. "
        "We release code and data for reproducibility.")
short = "Abstract. A new idea about solar panels. It works well."
for title, paper in [("paper A", good), ("paper B", short)]:
    print(title); bb = controller(paper)
    print("  blackboard:", json.dumps({k: v for k, v in bb.items() if k != "paper"}))

A pruned convolutional network is trained on 12,000 labelled images.", "status": "COMPLETED"}
